Recording a Partial Payment and a Goods Return Without Muddling the Balance

A retailer owes you Rs 18,500. On Tuesday they send Rs 7,000, and a week later they say some goods were returned. If you subtract both figures in one step and write only the new total, you lose the record of what happened. You also lose the chance to ask later why the balance changed.

This guide shows a manual way to keep the two events apart. The figures below come from a fictional worked example. It is not a real customer case, a news report, legal advice or evidence of business results [1].

The fictional example

An imaginary retailer has an opening amount payable of Rs 18,500. The distributor confirms a Rs 7,000 payment separately. The distributor also accepts a Rs 1,500 goods-return adjustment [1].

The remaining balance is 18,500 - 7,000 - 1,500 = 10,000 [1].

Keep a running balance, one line per event

Write each event on its own line and show the balance after each one:

Entry Type Amount (Rs) Balance after entry (Rs)
Opening amount payable Opening balance 18,500 18,500
Payment confirmed Money received 7,000 11,500
Goods return accepted Balance adjustment 1,500 10,000

Check each step:

  • 18,500 - 7,000 = 11,500
  • 11,500 - 1,500 = 10,000

A payment is money received. The goods return in this example is a separate balance adjustment [1]. Both reduce what the retailer owes, but only one is cash or a payment you can match to a payment record. That is why they need separate lines and separate labels.

What to write on every line

For each entry, keep the date, the amount, the customer's identity and the reason [1]. In practice that means:

  • Date: when the payment arrived or the return was agreed.
  • Amount: the exact figure, not a rounded one.
  • Customer: the retailer's name, plus any code you use to tell similar names apart.
  • Reason: "payment received" or "goods return accepted", with a short note such as the invoice it relates to.

Confirm before you mark money as received

Before you mark a payment as received, check it against the business's actual payment record [1]. If a retailer says they paid Rs 7,000 but you cannot find it in your own payment record, leave it out of the received column. Add a note that confirmation is pending. Enter it as a payment only once you can match it.

When the return is disputed

Suppose you do not agree that the Rs 1,500 of goods came back, or you do not agree on their value. The source says not to silently treat the adjustment as accepted [1].

The following is explanation, not source text. For this fictional exercise, note the disputed return in the ledger but do not subtract it until it is accepted. In the alternative fictional case, the table would look like this:

Entry Type Amount (Rs) Balance after entry (Rs)
Opening amount payable Opening balance 18,500 18,500
Payment confirmed Money received 7,000 11,500
Goods return claimed, disputed Not yet accepted 1,500 11,500

The balance stays at Rs 11,500 while the dispute is open. If the return is later accepted, add a dated line and the balance becomes 11,500 - 1,500 = 10,000. If it is rejected, record the reason beside the disputed line so the history stays readable.

A daily checklist

The source proposes these operational steps. They are suggestions, not legal requirements or a guarantee of faster collection [1]:

  1. Review new customer entries.
  2. Confirm that each payment belongs to the correct customer.
  3. Check the arithmetic.
  4. Identify disputed adjustments.
  5. Keep the remaining amount visible.
  6. Check the balance before sending a reminder.

Before sending a reminder in the disputed case, show the recorded payment and describe the Rs 1,500 return as unresolved. The ledger balance in this exercise remains Rs 11,500 pending agreement; do not describe that total as agreed by the customer.

A simple paper or spreadsheet layout

For a notebook or spreadsheet, a starting layout is one sheet per customer with these columns:

  • Date
  • Entry type (opening, payment, adjustment)
  • Reference (invoice number or payment reference)
  • Amount
  • Status (confirmed, pending, disputed, accepted)
  • Balance after entry
  • Reason or note

Recalculate the balance column by hand once at the end of each day. Compare the last balance with the figure you plan to quote to the customer.

Where software could fit

Bolcash is a pre-launch app for small agencies and distributors in India. The owner's planned release date is 20 November 2026. That is a plan, not proof of launch, so do not assume it is available today.

Its approved features include recording income and expenses and managing customer records. It can also scan receipts, extract text using OCR and display the extracted details for review. The extracted details and every financial entry still need your review. Nothing here means the app handles goods-return adjustments or confirms payments automatically, so keep the manual checks above in place whichever tool you use.

The point of the exercise

Separate lines for the opening balance, the confirmed payment and the accepted return let you explain how Rs 18,500 became Rs 10,000. If one line is challenged, you can show the date, amount, customer and reason for it without rebuilding the whole account.
